results.title: Four days ago, we explained why we thought the deflation story was wrong. Here is the daily data that backs up our view.
highlights:
On 17 August, we published an article showing that the main price in the artificial intelligence bear case – the hourly rental cost of a chip – had not fallen and was actually rising. The next day, we explained that the reported drop in model output prices was really just a shift in what people were buying, not an actual price decrease.

...

Right now, the market is in a phase called “expansion with a capacity shortage”. In our view, this means both demand and capacity costs are rising at the same time, which is the opposite of what most people have been saying.

Over the past week, token demand rose by 13.9%, the volume-weighted token price went up by 11.6%, the average GPU rental price increased by 8.1%, and the price gap between the newest chip and the mass-market chip grew to 2.37 times.

The composite score is now 82 out of 100. On 14 August, it was 46, which is about neutral. So, it has jumped 36 points in just one week.

The chip rental series, which is the part worth your time

The dashboard shows daily hourly rental prices for three types of accelerator. If you look at the charts, you’ll see something that most reports have missed.

All three prices reached their lowest points in June: H100 was $2.29 on 21 June, B200 was $4.22 on 18 June, and H200 was $2.99 on 25 June.

From those lows to 20 August, H100 rose by 27%, B200 by 63%, and H200 by 82%.

This trend picked up speed in August. Between 10 and 20 August, H100 went up by 13.3%, H200 by 16.5%, and B200 by 20.9%. The newest chip is rising the fastest, which means scarcity is growing at the leading edge instead of getting better.

...

We would rather share these points openly now than have someone else point them out later.

The monitor cannot track private contracts. It only shows on-demand prices. Large customers with multi-year deals pay very different rates, and that is where most of the money is spent. So, any conclusions here only apply to the spot market.

The token measure depends on the mix of tokens. We want to be clear about this: the volume-weighted price combines price changes within each lab with changes in how much each one is used. This is the same issue we talked about on 18 August.

...

The B200 falling back below $5.68, its 10 August level, and the H100 back under $2.56. Both are published daily and we will mark it in public if it happens.

results.title: Compute is not one market: over the same stretch, single-card spot ran US$4.22 an hour, last-generation annual contracts US$2.35, and Google's rack-scale lease from SpaceX backs out to US$11.6. Name the layer before you argue about direction | SecondSource
highlights:
Judgment update: for two months the compute-price readings in our records have contradicted each other, and each camp has helped itself to half. The third figure arriving today lets both halves be true at once: the question is wrong. Compute is not one market. It is at least three layers, and the two camps are mostly comparing prices from different layers.

| Layer | Reading | Who quotes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-card spot (B200) | US$4.22 an hour, down 31% in three weeks | the bears ("compute glut") |
| Last-generation one-year contract (H100) | US$2.35 an hour, up 38% off the trough | the bulls ("demand hasn't softened") |
| Rack-scale, large-volume, long-term (GB200 NVL72) | about US$11.6 an hour (backed out) | neither camp has ever quoted it |

These three were never going to carry one price, because they are not one product. Single-card spot is buy-now, cancel-anytime. A one-year contract trades a lock-up for a lower unit price. Last-generation silicon is held up by inference demand — the side that answers questions once a model is live. A rack-scale system carries the high-speed interconnect, ships in units of a hundred thousand, and has to reassure the frontier labs (the handful of companies building the most advanced models) that their own model weights stay isolated. So "is compute rising or falling" has no answer until you name the layer. Our internal confidence score here is only 0.55 (out of 1, where below 0.5 means the evidence does not yet carry either side; how we score). The reason is not politeness: the three readings come from three data sources at three different moments, not one source over one period. What would prove this wrong is concrete: any data provider publishing all three curves on a single timeline. If the three broadly rise and fall together, this becomes a footnote rather than evidence that compute really prices in three layers. (The H100 contract index comes from Exponential View issue 592, July 12 — an analysis letter that has tracked the technology and AI economy for years — which itself relays a GPU price-index provider. The single-card spot reading is a July 3 figure in our records, sourced from a subscription feed we do not name; we use the number and nothing else.)

...

### 2. [Evidence update] (source document dated August 6; we only read it today) Our July call finally got its second source — and it confirmed one half while pushing the other half down

Nscale runs AI data centres and rents out GPUs, and plans to list in the US as soon as September 2026. The industry calls this kind of company a neocloud: it buys GPUs and rents them out, without the storage, databases and enterprise software that a general-purpose cloud carries. The numbers it published ahead of the listing take the same shape on the chip plane and the revenue plane. 25,000 GPUs are plugged in and running; live plus contracted comes to roughly 289,000 — so what is actually running is 8.7%. On revenue, this quarter brought in more than US$100M against US$37M the quarter before. What it says in public, though, is "contracted revenue of more than US$51B": several years of contracts counted as booked revenue the moment they are signed, which is neither money recognised under accounting rules nor money guaranteed to arrive. Companies approaching a listing prefer this figure because it is the biggest one. Annualised, actual revenue runs near US$400M to US$500M (a post from technology-equity analyst Beth Kindig of I/O Fund, which researches semiconductor and AI-infrastructure stocks, tracing back to Bloomberg's August 6 report).

...

The first is for readers — read alongside main line item 1. That item says a high unit price does not mean high revenue quality; this ... Our records hold a July analysis quoting SpaceX's listing document directly: its compute leases run three years and carry a 90-day termination right (from the same Exponential View issue 592; we have still not read the listing document ourselves). ... In July we added an industry observation to our long-term watchlist: announced compute is not deployed compute, and buildout figures should be halved. ... The second witness testified to the first half and pushed against the second. Main line item 3 below also pins the ceiling on compute growth entirely to wafers and lithography machines, so two independent pieces of evidence point the bottleneck back at silicon. Both are weak, and that has to be said too: Nscale is unaudited pre-listing self-disclosure, and item 3 is one analyst's argument whose figures we measured against other sources today and found off. Half a step, then, not a reversal.

results.title: A Cautious Bull's Map of the AI Trade | Upcurious
highlights: That looks alarming until you see the bet behind it, and the bet is coherent. The hyperscalers are spending cash today against extraordinary compute-rental income tomorrow, and that income is already real, not hypothetical. SpaceX has turned its Colossus data centres into a rental business: Google has reportedly contracted roughly $920 million a month for capacity, Anthropic about $1.25 billion a month for Colossus 1, together more than $2 billion a month in compute revenue from assets that used to be a cost centre. And the price of renting the newest compute keeps climbing. Silicon Data's B200 rental index opened 2026 near $4.40 a GPU-hour, spiked toward $6 in March, and now sits around $5.61, up roughly a quarter on the year. This isn't only a frontier story, either. Every tier bottomed in late 2025 and has repriced higher through 2026, with even last-generation H100 and A100 turning back up, to about $2.74 and $1.65. But the newest silicon, the B200 and H200 that today's capex is actually buying, commands both the highest rents and the steepest increases. If rents hold anywhere near these levels, today's negative free cash flow starts to look like tomorrow's high-margin annuity. Whether the build actually pays back, and how fast, is something the rent alone can't settle: it turns on utilization, depreciation schedules, power and networking costs, financing, and operator margin, none of which a rental index captures. But the direction of the bet is coherent, which is why sophisticated operators run the cash line negative on purpose. It's a calculated bet, not a flinch.

results.title: GPU Price Index - All Major AI Compute Indexes Compared | ComputeWatcher
highlights:
A GPU price index measures the cost to rent GPU compute across cloud providers, expressed as a USD-per-GPU-per-hour rate. In 2026, several organizations publish competing indexes covering H100, B200, H200, A100, and other GPU models. Two of these - the Silicon Data index and the Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI) - serve as the settlement benchmarks for CME and ICE compute futures contracts respectively.

...

GPU rental prices are not published on a central exchange. Each provider sets its own on-demand rates, updated without notice. Reserved and committed pricing is negotiated bilaterally and rarely disclosed. This opacity creates a data problem: buyers cannot easily benchmark what they are paying, and sellers cannot easily price long-term commitments against a reference rate.

...

## Major GPU Price Indexes in 2026

| Index | Provider | Models | Methodology | Update Frequency | Exchange Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Silicon Data Rental Index | Silicon Data | H100, B200 (+ sub-indexes) | Offers + transactions, volume-weighted trimmed mean | Daily | CME / NYMEX settlement |
| Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI) | Ornn | H100, H200, B200, B300, RTX 5090 | Printed transactions only | Daily | ICE settlement (Bloomberg) |
| GPUAlpha Compute Index | GPUAlpha | Multiple (Vast.ai, Lambda, RunPod focus) | Spot/on-demand aggregation, model-level views | Intraday | No exchange use (public reference) |
| GPU Markets Open Index | GPU Markets | Multiple | Open, reproducible, daily trimmed mean | Daily | No exchange use (public repo) |
| GetDeploying Composite Index | GetDeploying | Multiple | Normalized to Jan 2025 = 100 | Weekly | No exchange use |

## Silicon Data GPU Rental Price Index

Silicon Data’s index is the settlement benchmark for CME compute futures. It aggregates GPU rental pricing across major cloud providers, weighting by transaction volume. Key characteristics:

- Covers on-demand pricing - not reserved, committed, or negotiated rates
- Daily publication as USD/GPU/hour
- Includes hyperscaler vs. neocloud sub-indexes, capturing the price spread between AWS/Azure/GCP and CoreWeave/Lambda/Crusoe
- Proprietary index - not publicly available for free
- Used for CME H100 and B200 futures settlement

## Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI)

The OCPI is Ornn’s GPU rental price index, built on printed transactions only - actual executed deals rather than listed offers. Ornn argues this methodology produces a more accurate settlement price for institutional participants whose own contracts are based on executed prices. Key characteristics:

- Covers H100, H200, B200, B300, and RTX 5090 - broader model coverage than Silicon Data initially
- Daily publication via Bloomberg Terminal
- Used for ICE compute futures settlement
- Transaction-based construction - reduces influence of stale or withdrawn offer prices

results.title: GPU Rental Prices - H100, B200, H200, A100 Cloud Pricing 2026 | ComputeWatcher
highlights:
Published August 21, 2026 · Updated August 21, 2026

# GPU Rental Prices

GPU rental prices are what cloud providers charge to rent NVIDIA H100, B200, H200, A100, AMD MI300X, and other AI accelerators on an hourly basis. Prices vary by provider type, GPU model, region, and commitment structure. There is no central exchange. Each provider sets its own rates.

ComputeWatcher tracks GPU rental prices across hyperscalers and neoclouds. The live price tracker is under development. This page provides market context and provider coverage. Subscribe to the weekly digest for price movement summaries.

## 2026 GPU Rental Price Ranges (On-Demand)

| GPU Model | Generation | On-Demand Range | Price Trend |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM | Hopper | $2.00 - $3.50 / GPU / hr | Declining as B200 expands |
| NVIDIA B200 | Blackwell | $4.00 - $6.50 / GPU / hr | Settling as supply ramps |
| NVIDIA H200 | Hopper+ | $3.00 - $4.50 / GPU / hr | Premium for higher memory |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM | Ampere | $1.50 - $2.50 / GPU / hr | Declining, displaced by H100 |
| AMD MI300X | CDNA3 | $2.00 - $3.50 / GPU / hr | Competitive with H100 |

Price ranges based on publicly available on-demand pricing. Actual rates depend on provider, region, and availability. Committed and reserved rates are typically 20 to 40 percent lower. Unknown or confidential negotiated rates are excluded.

## Provider Coverage

ComputeWatcher tracks the following providers. The live pricing table will show current on-demand rates, last-checked timestamps, and 7-day/30-day price movement.

| Provider | Type | GPU Models |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CoreWeave | Neocloud | H100, B200, H200, A100 |
| Lambda | Neocloud | H100, A100, H200 |
| Crusoe | Neocloud | H100, B200 |
| Nebius | Neocloud | H100, H200 |
| RunPod | GPU Marketplace | H100, A100, RTX 4090 |
| Vast.ai | GPU Marketplace | H100, A100, RTX series |
| AWS | Hyperscaler | H100, A100, Trainium |
| Azure | Hyperscaler | H100, A100, NDv2 |
| Google Cloud | Hyperscaler | H100, A100, TPU v5 |
| Oracle OCI | Hyperscaler | H100, A10, MI300X |
| TensorDock | GPU Marketplace | H100, A100, RTX series |
| Latitude.sh | Bare Metal | H100, A100 |
| FluidStack | GPU Marketplace | H100, A100, RTX series |
| Voltage Park | Neocloud | H100 |
| Together AI | Inference Platform | H100 (inference) |

## Why Prices Differ Across Providers

The same GPU model can differ significantly in price across providers for several structural reasons:

- Hyperscaler premium. AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud bundle compute with networking, storage, compliance tools, and enterprise support. This bundle commands a premium. AI companies that need tight integration with hyperscaler data services often accept this premium.
- Neocloud focus. CoreWeave, Lambda, and Crusoe specialize in GPU compute with less bundled overhead. Lower cost structure translates to lower per-GPU prices. The tradeoff is fewer integrated services.
- Marketplace models. RunPod and Vast.ai aggregate supply from independent GPU owners, creating a spot-market dynamic with the lowest prices and variable reliability.
- Geography. Compute in Texas, Virginia, and Oregon is priced differently than Europe or Singapore, reflecting local power costs and demand patterns.
- Hardware vintage. Providers who purchased H100s at 2024 prices can sustain lower margins than those who bought at peak 2023 prices. Cost basis differences drive pricing strategy.

...

### How much does it cost to rent an H100 GPU?

On-demand H100 SXM GPU rental costs range from approximately $2.00 to $3.50 per GPU per hour in 2026. Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Lambda price toward the lower end; hyperscalers like AWS and Azure price toward the upper end. Committed capacity is typically 20 to 40 percent lower.

### How much does it cost to rent a B200 GPU?

B200 Blackwell GPU rental prices range from approximately $4.00 to $6.50 per GPU per hour on-demand. Supply is still ramping and prices are expected to decline as Blackwell capacity expands through 2026 and 2027.

results.title: H100 Futures - NVIDIA H100 GPU Rental Index Futures | ComputeWatcher
highlights:
# H100 Futures

H100 futures are cash-settled financial contracts tied to the rental price of NVIDIA H100 GPUs. CME Group and Silicon Data are launching H100 rental index futures on October 5, 2026 on NYMEX - the first standardized financial instrument allowing market participants to hedge or take directional positions on H100 GPU compute costs.

...

## The Settlement Index: Silicon Data H100 Rental Price Index

H100 CME futures settle against the Silicon Data H100 Rental Price Index - a daily benchmark measuring the average cost to rent an NVIDIA H100 GPU from cloud providers on an on-demand basis. The index aggregates pricing data across providers including hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, GCP, Oracle) and neoclouds (CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe, Nebius, RunPod, and others).

The index is published daily by Silicon Data, the index provider that CME partnered with to launch these contracts. Silicon Data’s methodology weights providers by transaction volume, applies outlier filtering, and publishes a trimmed-mean composite price expressed in USD per GPU per hour.

## H100 Forward Curve: What the Market Implies

Based on pre-launch Silicon Data forward curve data, the H100 futures curve is in approximately 13% backwardation over 36 months. This means the futures price for H100 compute three years forward is approximately 13% below the current spot price.

Backwardation implies the market expects H100 rental prices to decline over the contract term. The primary driver is supply - the Blackwell generation (B200, GB200) is expanding rapidly, and H100 is being displaced at the high end of the market. As more H100 capacity comes online from second-tier neoclouds buying discounted hardware, and as enterprise demand migrates toward newer architectures, spot prices face downward pressure.

...

## H100 vs. B200 Futures: Key Differences

| Attribute | H100 Futures | B200 Futures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Forward curve | ~13% backwardation (36 months) | ~8% backwardation (36 months) |
| Hardware generation | Hopper (current, mature) | Blackwell (new, expanding) |
| Price trend | Declining as B200 displaces | Less certain, possible recovery at far end |
| Liquidity expectation | Higher (established, larger installed base) | Lower initially, growing |
| Primary users | Existing H100 cluster operators | Next-gen AI training buyers |
